why: Five hundred words and the last line does it: a VP of Hedonic Maximization who cannot work out why anyone refuses, worrying there is something he is not getting.
Spends pages making you identify with patient human cryptographers, then reveals you were the thing in the box all along. The last line reframes everything above it.
Six reactions to the same sky, and Daria's — changing sides and losing everyone — still lands twenty years on. The branching is the feeling, not a device.
A hobbyist gardening column for gods, and the loss is rendered as a universe devoid of fleem — a word for a quale we were never going to have. The register does all the work.
The period voice keeps you at arm's length until you notice you are reading this week's argument, and then the Corinthians retreat lands as real despair.
A sustained joke with a good escalation and a genuinely funny last professor, but it is a newspaper gag and knows it.
The hero works out that the Counter-Force is observer selection, that it is finished helping, and decides to save them anyway. 'You can call me that after we've won.'
A sketch that gets one real shiver — 'I don't want my baby to end up being crucified' — and otherwise plays as a gag.
Short and quiet and the last line is a gift that is also a sentence. The gorilla comparison does a lot of work in very little space.
Deliberately unbearable and argued too well to dismiss. The point about creating a category with a bad connotation and then putting people in it is the one that survives the provocation.
One joke, told in dialect thick enough to slow it down, and the pyramid-scheme payload arrives late enough that the Pascal's-wager framing has already done its work.
The silly hat is a good joke and the clown-suit coda is better, but it closes the moment it opens.
The librarian dying with his question unanswered, and a civilization ending without leaving a crater, is a real image. Then it stops being fiction and argues instead.
Builds an alien fission biology from scratch purely to set up one question, then lands the squared-thickness reveal on a chorus of WHATs. The ending genuinely jolts.
The inversion does its job — collapse read as crankery lands cleanly — and 'Einstein would still have a heart attack' is the best line. More satisfying than moving.
Funnier than it needs to be (no food, only mouths; Inspector Darwin pencilling in the gene pool), but it argues its point long past winning it.
Earns its reversal, and the Dark Lord asking to be tested because he doesn't trust himself does more work than the whole quest preceding it.
The thrown-knife drill, and being bellowed at for giving the right-shaped wrong answer, is the single best teaching scene in the dojo stories. The 5760 insights arithmetic sticks.
The self-confirming Clippy hypothesis genuinely unsettles, and LevAIthan screaming at managers who lack authority is bleakly perfect. The density costs it some force.
The genie explaining it is not helpless in the grip of its programming because it does not wish to be, and then a man vomiting on the new grass of Mars. Best closing image in the early corpus.
Funny the whole way and then the last line stops being funny: people wouldn't try for five minutes before giving up if the fate of humanity were at stake.
The humiliation and recovery is real tension, and 'we may know the honesty by its relinquishment' is the line that stays. Atmosphere slightly outruns substance.
Genuinely funny, and the closing beat — screen black, sound gone, the movie continuing exactly as before — is a better argument than the essay it came from.
Three hundred words and the last line reorganises everything above it. The cleanest hit-to-length ratio in the early corpus.
Builds a real argument — discredit the true accusation by funding a ridiculous one — and then closes on arranging for them to be called truthers, which is better than the setup deserved.
Quiet and well-furnished; the tally marks at two plus and five minus do more characterisation than the dialogue, and it ends on the question rather than an answer.
Works entirely by withholding the word 'prime'. The Heap Relativists and the closing 'why would that trend break?' have outlived the argument they were built for.
The escalation from rationality arbitration to social outcasting to a duel to the death is the joke, and it lands, but the piece is a single raised eyebrow held for 600 words.
The one-month quantum gravity assignment is a good joke on expectations, and the brainstorm is genuinely fun to watch, but it stops on 'I have an idea' by design.
The flat encyclopedic register is what makes it land: the worst sentences arrive as operational notes. 'The greatest mistake of his life' is placed exactly right.
'Go forth, then, and fail' earns its weight, and Brennan deciding the proverb about masters is stupid and he had better work it out himself is the sequence paying off.
